statutes.title: Security Deposit — Application and Definition
statutes.summary: Defines security deposit and establishes that the chapter applies to all residential leases in Texas.

key_provisions.description: Defines 'security deposit' as any advance of money, other than a rental application deposit or an advance payment of rent, intended primarily to secure performance under a lease.

statutes.title: Obligation to Refund
statutes.summary: Requires the landlord to refund the security deposit (less lawful deductions) within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises AND provides a written statement of the tenant's forwarding address.

key_provisions.description: Landlord must return the deposit within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises. The duty to refund does not arise until the tenant provides the landlord with a written statement of the tenant's forwarding address for purposes of refund.

statutes.title: Retention of Security Deposit; Accounting
statutes.summary: Allows landlord to deduct for damages and charges beyond normal wear and tear, breach of lease, and unpaid rent. Must provide written description and itemized list of deductions.

key_provisions.description: Landlord may not retain any portion of the deposit to cover normal wear and tear.
If landlord retains any portion, must give tenant the balance along with a written description and itemized list of all deductions.
Landlord is not obligated to return deposit until tenant gives a forwarding address.

statutes.title: Liability of Landlord — Bad Faith Retention
statutes.summary: A landlord who in bad faith retains the security deposit is liable for an amount equal to the sum of $100, three times the portion wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney's fees.

key_provisions.description: Landlord who in bad faith retains a security deposit in violation of this subchapter is liable for $100 + 3x the portion of the deposit wrongfully withheld + reasonable attorney's fees in a suit to recover the deposit.

deadline_rules.action_at_expiry: Landlord must return deposit or provide written itemized deductions (requires tenant to have provided forwarding address)
deadline_rules.description: Texas law requires the landlord to return your security deposit (or provide an itemized statement of deductions) within 30 days after you surrender the premises AND provide a written forwarding address.
deadline_rules.prompt_message: The 30-day deadline for your landlord to return your deposit or provide an itemized statement has passed. People in this situation in Texas typically send a demand letter citing Tex. Prop. Code §92.103.

deadline_rules.action_at_expiry: If no response to demand letter, consider filing in Justice Court
deadline_rules.description: If your landlord has not responded to your demand letter within 30 days, people in similar situations typically consider filing in Justice Court.
deadline_rules.prompt_message: It's been 30 days since you sent your demand letter. If you haven't received a response, people in similar situations in Texas typically consider filing in Justice Court. We can help you prepare the filing packet.

penalties.description: Bad faith retention: $100 + three times the portion of the deposit wrongfully withheld + reasonable attorney's fees.
penalties.amount_or_formula: $100 + (3 x wrongfully withheld amount) + reasonable attorney's fees
penalties.conditions: Requires showing landlord acted in bad faith. Bad faith is established by the failure to return the deposit or provide an itemization within the 30-day period.

escalation_venues.name: Texas Justice Court (Small Claims)
escalation_venues.description: Texas Justice Courts hear small claims up to $20,000. Filing fees vary by county, typically $54-$100+. E-filing available via eFileTexas.gov.

escalation_venues.name: Texas Attorney General — Consumer Protection
escalation_venues.description: File a consumer complaint with the Texas Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division.

permissible_deductions.name: Damages and Charges Beyond Normal Wear and Tear
permissible_deductions.description: Landlord may deduct for damages and charges for which the tenant is legally liable under the lease or as a result of breaching the lease, excluding normal wear and tear.
permissible_deductions.typical_dispute_basis: Normal wear and tear is explicitly excluded; landlord must provide itemized list

permissible_deductions.name: Unpaid Rent
permissible_deductions.typical_dispute_basis: Dispute the amount; show evidence of payment

permissible_deductions.name: Charges for Breach of Lease
permissible_deductions.description: Landlord may deduct for charges resulting from breach of lease (e.g., early termination fees if in the lease).
permissible_deductions.typical_dispute_basis: Dispute the breach; argue the charge is not a legitimate deduction

permissible_deductions.name: Normal Wear and Tear
permissible_deductions.description: Landlord may NOT retain any portion of the security deposit to cover normal wear and tear.
permissible_deductions.typical_dispute_basis: Statute explicitly prohibits deductions for normal wear and tear

special_provisions.title: Forwarding Address Required to Trigger Deadline
special_provisions.description: Critical Texas-specific provision: the landlord's 30-day obligation to return the deposit does NOT begin until the tenant provides a written statement of their forwarding address. If no forwarding address was provided, the landlord has a defense for not returning the deposit.
special_provisions.conditions: Always applicable — letter should reference the forwarding address and when it was provided

special_provisions.title: No Statutory Deposit Cap
special_provisions.description: Texas does not limit the amount a landlord can charge as a security deposit. The amount is determined by the lease.
special_provisions.statute_ref: Tex. Prop. Code §92.101 et seq. (no cap provision)

notes: Texas is moderately tenant-friendly on deposits. The 3x bad-faith penalty is strong but requires showing bad faith. The forwarding-address requirement is a critical nuance — many tenants don't know the 30-day clock doesn't start until they provide it in writing. Texas has no statutory cap on deposit amounts. Justice Court limit of $20,000 is unusually high for small claims, which is favorable.
